title: Answer the product manager
prompt: `products` is loaded with `product_id` as its index. Set `grinder_price` to the unit price of product 7. Set `subset` to products 11, 21 and 37 with only the `name` and `unit_cost` columns, in that order. Set `top5` to the five most expensive products with all their columns, most expensive first. Set `cheapest_name` to the name of the cheapest product.
hints: Product 7 is a label, so use `.loc[7, "unit_price"]`.
`.loc` takes a list of row labels and a list of column names: `.loc[[11, 21, 37], ["name", "unit_cost"]]`.

Sort with `products.sort_values("unit_price", ascending=False)`, then take positions with `.iloc[:5]`. The cheapest product is at position `-1` of that sorted table (or position 0 of an ascending sort).
explanation: Product ids are labels, so `.loc` is the right tool for questions 1 and 2, and it returns the columns in the order you list them. "The five most expensive" is about position after sorting, so `.iloc[:5]` on the sorted table is the natural fit; `nlargest(5, "unit_price")`, which you meet next lesson, also works. The cheapest product is the Jump Rope Pro at 18 dollars. Notice that `.loc[1:5]` on the sorted table would not give the top five: it would return whatever rows sit between labels 1 and 5 in their new positions, which has nothing to do with price.

checks.subset: `subset` has products 11, 21, 37 and the columns name, unit_cost
checks.top5: `top5` holds the five highest prices in descending order
